study.title: Psalm 91 - Refuge, Care and Salvation of God
study.overview: Psalm 91 presents the assurance of those who make the Lord his dwelling. The poem alternates confession of confidence, promises of protection, and the final divine response. The text does not promise a life without conflict, but states that God keeps his people, sustains his faith in the midst of danger and ultimately grants life and salvation. The emphasis lies less on human autonomy and more in inhabiting God, trusting in him and receiving from him protection, deliverance and honor.

outline.title: The abode of the Most High and the Confession of Trust
outline.explanation: The psalm begins with the image of someone living near God, in the shadow of the Almighty. Then the personal voice declares the Lord as a refuge, strength and object of trust. The central idea is of communion and dependence, not just occasional help.

outline.title: Protection against visible and invisible threats
outline.explanation: Here are varied dangers: traps, diseases, night terror, daytime violence and the judgment of the wicked. The point is not to deny the existence of evil, but to affirm that the faithful does not need to be dominated by fear, because the Lord watches over him and his goodness creates hope in the midst of distress.

outline.title: The promise to those who make the Lord their dwelling
outline.explanation: The text repeats the idea of inhabiting the Lord and broadens the promises of protection. Divine intervention includes commanding angels to guard the ways of the righteous. The image of lion and serpent pawn shows dominion over hostile forces and symbolizes victory granted by God.

outline.title: God's answer: deliverance, presence and salvation
outline.explanation: In conclusion, God speaks directly about the love and knowledge of his name by the faithful. He promises deliverance, presence in anguish, honor and satisfaction with long life. The culmination is the vision of divine salvation, which goes beyond mere physical preservation.

study.context: The notes received treat the psalm as a song of wisdom and trust, possibly linked to divine protection in times of danger. Matthew Henry mentions that some ancients attributed him to Moses, but considers it likely to author authorship, but this is presented only as probability, not as a certainty of the text. Adam Clarke notes that the psalm has no Hebrew title and that his occasion and authorship cannot be safely determined. The notes also point out that this psalm functions as a kind of declaration of protection for those who trust in God.
study.theology: The psalm teaches that the security of God's people is born to remain in him. The language of refuge, shadow, strength and housing indicates continuous relationship, not just emergency help. Promises of deliverance should not be read as a guarantee of total absence of problems; Tyndale's own note recalls that they do not ensure escape from every tribulation, but create expectation of the Lord's goodness. Angels appear as servants commissioned by God, and not as recipients of worship. The conclusion shows that the greater good is not only to survive, but to be preserved, honored, and led to God's salvation. In evangelical reading, this points to the Lord's fidelity to sustaining his, calling them in anguish and leading them to a full life under his grace.

scholarViews.insight: The psalm expresses confidence in the Almighty God, who offers shelter to those who take refuge in him; the psalmist teaches that divine protection does not mean absence of trial, but trust in the goodness of the Lord.
The image of dwelling in the hiding place of the Most High describes the true believer as one who is at home in God, rests on him and finds in him what he needs.
The text on angels should be understood as God's providential care: they receive order from him and should not be the object of prayer or praise.

questions: What does it mean, in practice, to inhabit the Lord and not just ask him for help in difficult times?
How to maintain faith and serenity when the text promises protection, but does the Christian experience still include suffering and risk?
In what way does the final promise of salvation correct a narrow vision of blessing centered only on material security?
study.practice: This week, turn the psalm into daily prayer: identify concrete fears, give them to the Lord as your refuge and ask for your confidence in him to be greater than your anxiety. It is also worth practicing spiritual vigilance, remembering that the care of God does not dispense obedience, discernment and humility. In facing news, illnesses or threats, recite the central truth of the psalm: God does not abandon those who shelter in it, and their salvation is greater than the present danger.
study.uncertainty: Notes do not allow the safety of authorship, historical occasion or a specific identification of the dangers described in the psalm. Nor is it possible to affirm that promises should be read as a guarantee of physical deliverance in any case; the notes themselves warn that there are real afflictions and that the emphasis rests on God's faithfulness and the expectation of his goodness.
